Dynamic Optimal Transport

Optimal transport becomes especially powerful once distances between measures are seen as actions of moving mass. This chapter first develops the dynamic language: continuity equations describe admissible measure evolutions, while the Benamou--Brenier formula identifies W2\Wass_2W2​ with a least-action principle. These ideas prepare the gradient-flow and generative-model chapters that follow.

Guiding Comparison

The static formulation optimizes over a coupling between endpoints. The dynamic formulation optimizes over a whole path of measures and a velocity field. The continuity equation is the constraint, and kinetic energy is the cost.

Evolutions Over the Space of Measures¶

We start with the continuity equation because it is the common language for particles, densities and weak measure evolutions. It also makes precise which velocity fields actually move mass.

Lagrangian and Eulerian Descriptions¶

Consider an evolution t↦αt∈P(Rd)t\mapsto\alpha_t\in\mathcal P(\RR^d)t↦αt​∈P(Rd). It can be described in a Lagrangian way as the advection of particles along a time-dependent vector field vt(x)v_t(x)vt​(x):

 dx(t) dt=vt(x(t)).\frac{\d x(t)}{\d t}=v_t(x(t)).dtdx(t)​=vt​(x(t)).
(1)

Writing TtT_tTt​ for the associated flow map, so that Tt(x(0))=x(t)T_t(x(0))=x(t)Tt​(x(0))=x(t), the advected measure is

αt=(Tt)♯α0.\alpha_t=(T_t)_\sharp\alpha_0.αt​=(Tt​)♯​α0​.
(2)

For empirical measures, αt=n−1∑i=1nδxi(t)\alpha_t=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i(t)}αt​=n−1∑i=1n​δxi​(t)​, each particle solves (1).

In the Eulerian description, the same motion is written directly on the evolving measure:

∂αt∂t+div⁡(vtαt)=0.\frac{\partial\alpha_t}{\partial t} +\operatorname{div}(v_t\alpha_t)=0.∂t∂αt​​+div(vt​αt​)=0.
(3)

This PDE is often called the advection equation, the continuity equation, or Liouville’s equation when it acts on phase space. It is a classical PDE only when αt\alpha_tαt​ has a smooth density. For general measures, and in particular for empirical measures, it is understood weakly: for any smooth test function (t,x)↦φ(t,x)(t,x)\mapsto\varphi(t,x)(t,x)↦φ(t,x) compactly supported in time,

∫01 ⁣∫Rd(∂tφ(t,x)+⟨vt(x),∇xφ(t,x)⟩) dαt(x) dt=0.\int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d} \left( \partial_t\varphi(t,x) +\dotp{v_t(x)}{\nabla_x\varphi(t,x)} \right) \d\alpha_t(x)\d t =0.∫01​∫Rd​(∂t​φ(t,x)+⟨vt​(x),∇x​φ(t,x)⟩)dαt​(x)dt=0.
(4)

This weak equation is obtained from (3) by integration by parts. For smooth positive densities, the classical and weak formulations are equivalent; for particle clouds, the weak form remains meaningful.

Proposition: Lagrangian Flows Solve the Continuity Equation

Consider a smooth flow Tt:Rd→RdT_t:\RR^d\to\RR^dTt​:Rd→Rd and define αt=(Tt)♯α0\alpha_t=(T_t)_\sharp\alpha_0αt​=(Tt​)♯​α0​. Define the Eulerian velocity field by

vt(Tt(y))=∂tTt(y).v_t(T_t(y))=\partial_t T_t(y).vt​(Tt​(y))=∂t​Tt​(y).
(5)

Then (αt,vt)(\alpha_t,v_t)(αt​,vt​) solves the continuity equation in the weak sense (4). In particular, if α0=n−1∑iδxi(0)\alpha_0=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(0)}α0​=n−1∑i​δxi​(0)​ is empirical, then αt=n−1∑iδxi(t)\alpha_t=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(t)}αt​=n−1∑i​δxi​(t)​ is empirical as well, with particle velocities x˙i(t)=vt(xi(t))\dot x_i(t)=v_t(x_i(t))x˙i​(t)=vt​(xi​(t)).

Let φ(t,x)\varphi(t,x)φ(t,x) be a smooth test function vanishing at t=0t=0t=0 and t=1t=1t=1. Since αt=(Tt)♯α0\alpha_t=(T_t)_\sharp\alpha_0αt​=(Tt​)♯​α0​,

 d dt∫φ(t,x) dαt(x)= d dt∫φ(t,Tt(y)) dα0(y).\frac{\d}{\d t}\int \varphi(t,x)\d\alpha_t(x) = \frac{\d}{\d t}\int \varphi(t,T_t(y))\d\alpha_0(y).dtd​∫φ(t,x)dαt​(x)=dtd​∫φ(t,Tt​(y))dα0​(y).

The chain rule gives

From Measure Evolutions to Vector Fields¶

For a given evolution (αt)t(\alpha_t)_t(αt​)t​, there are typically infinitely many velocity fields vtv_tvt​ satisfying

∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0.\partial_t\alpha_t+\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)=0.∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0.
(9)

This non-uniqueness comes from the kernel of the weighted divergence. The linear space of vector fields that leave a measure α\alphaα invariant is

Hα={v:div⁡(αv)=0}.\mathcal H_\alpha = \{v:\operatorname{div}(\alpha v)=0\}.Hα​={v:div(αv)=0}.
(10)

It is usually non-trivial: if α\alphaα is an isotropic Gaussian, Hα\mathcal H_\alphaHα​ contains rotational vector fields generated by anti-symmetric matrices.

Dacorogna--Moser Inversion¶

Reconstructing particles from an observed density evolution is therefore ill-posed. A simple choice, introduced by Dacorogna and Moser Dacorogna & Moser, 1990, imposes that the flux αtvt\alpha_t v_tαt​vt​ is a gradient field. Formally,

vt=−1αt∇Δ−1(∂tαt),v_t = -\frac{1}{\alpha_t} \nabla\Delta^{-1}(\partial_t\alpha_t),vt​=−αt​1​∇Δ−1(∂t​αt​),
(11)

with suitable boundary conditions, for instance vanishing at infinity. This formula is useful conceptually but delicate when αt\alpha_tαt​ vanishes, and it does not generally produce a gradient velocity field.

The classical Dacorogna--Moser construction uses the linear density path. If αi=ρi  dx\alpha_i=\rho_i\,\d xαi​=ρi​dx are smooth positive densities with the same total mass on a bounded domain Ω\OmegaΩ, set

αt=(1−t)α0+tα1=ρt  dx,ρt=(1−t)ρ0+tρ1.\alpha_t=(1-t)\alpha_0+t\alpha_1=\rho_t\,\d x, \qquad \rho_t=(1-t)\rho_0+t\rho_1.αt​=(1−t)α0​+tα1​=ρt​dx,ρt​=(1−t)ρ0​+tρ1​.
(12)

Choose a time-independent flux www satisfying

div⁡w=ρ0−ρ1,w⋅n=0on ∂Ω,\operatorname{div} w=\rho_0-\rho_1, \qquad w\cdot n=0\quad\hbox{on }\partial\Omega,divw=ρ0​−ρ1​,w⋅n=0on ∂Ω,
(13)

for instance w=−∇ϕw=-\nabla\phiw=−∇ϕ with Δϕ=ρ1−ρ0\Delta\phi=\rho_1-\rho_0Δϕ=ρ1​−ρ0​ and Neumann boundary condition. Then

vt=wρtv_t=\frac{w}{\rho_t}vt​=ρt​w​
(14)

satisfies ∂tρt+div⁡(ρtvt)=0\partial_t\rho_t+\operatorname{div}(\rho_t v_t)=0∂t​ρt​+div(ρt​vt​)=0. The flow ∂tTt=vt∘Tt\partial_t T_t=v_t\circ T_t∂t​Tt​=vt​∘Tt​, T0=Id⁡T_0=\operatorname{Id}T0​=Id, therefore transports ρ0 dx\rho_0\d xρ0​dx onto ρt dx\rho_t\d xρt​dx, and T1T_1T1​ solves the prescribed-Jacobian problem ρ1(T1(x))det⁡(∇T1(x))=ρ0(x)\rho_1(T_1(x))\det(\nabla T_1(x))=\rho_0(x)ρ1​(T1​(x))det(∇T1​(x))=ρ0​(x).

Least-Square Inversion and Gradient Structure¶

A more robust choice, used implicitly in flow matching, optimal transport and Wasserstein gradient flows, is to select among all admissible velocities the one with smallest kinetic energy:

min⁡v12∫01 ⁣∫Rd∥vt(x)∥2  dαt(x) dtsubject to∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0.\min_v \frac12\int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d}\norm{v_t(x)}^2\,\d\alpha_t(x)\d t \quad \text{subject to} \quad \partial_t\alpha_t+\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)=0.vmin​21​∫01​∫Rd​∥vt​(x)∥2dαt​(x)dtsubject to∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0.
(15)
Proposition: Least-Square Velocities Are Gradients

Assume that αt=ρt  dx\alpha_t=\rho_t\,\d xαt​=ρt​dx is a smooth positive density curve and that boundary terms vanish. The minimizer of (15), if it exists, is a gradient field

vt=∇ϕt,v_t=\nabla\phi_t,vt​=∇ϕt​,
(16)

where ϕt\phi_tϕt​, unique up to an additive constant, solves the weighted Poisson equation

−div⁡(ρt∇ϕt)=∂tρt,vt=−∇Δαt−1(∂tαt),Δαtϕ=div⁡(αt∇ϕ).-\operatorname{div}(\rho_t\nabla\phi_t)=\partial_t\rho_t, \qquad v_t=-\nabla\Delta_{\alpha_t}^{-1}(\partial_t\alpha_t), \qquad \Delta_{\alpha_t}\phi=\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t\nabla\phi).−div(ρt​∇ϕt​)=∂t​ρt​,vt​=−∇Δαt​−1​(∂t​αt​),Δαt​​ϕ=div(αt​∇ϕ).
(17)
Proof

Introduce a Lagrange multiplier ϕt\phi_tϕt​ for the continuity equation. The constrained problem has the formal saddle formulation

min⁡vmax⁡ϕ∫01[12∫Rd∥vt(x)∥2  dαt(x)+∫Rdϕt(x)(div⁡(αtvt)(x)+∂tαt(x)) dx] dt.\min_v\max_\phi \int_0^1 \left[ \frac12\int_{\RR^d}\norm{v_t(x)}^2\,\d\alpha_t(x) + \int_{\RR^d}\phi_t(x) \left(\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)(x)+\partial_t\alpha_t(x)\right) \d x \right]\d t.vmin​ϕmax​∫01​[21​∫Rd​∥vt​(x)∥2dαt​(x)+∫Rd​ϕt​(x)(div(αt​vt​)(x)+∂t​αt​(x))dx]dt.
(18)

Integrating by parts in the divergence term gives, for each ttt,

∫(12∥vt∥2−⟨∇ϕt,vt⟩) dαt+∫ϕt ∂tαt.\int \left( \frac12\norm{v_t}^2-\dotp{\nabla\phi_t}{v_t} \right) \d\alpha_t + \int\phi_t\,\partial_t\alpha_t.∫(21​∥vt​∥2−⟨∇ϕt​,vt​⟩)dαt​+∫ϕt​∂t​αt​.
(19)

The pointwise minimizer in vtv_tvt​ is therefore vt=∇ϕtv_t=\nabla\phi_tvt​=∇ϕt​. Substituting this into ∂tρt+div⁡(ρtvt)=0\partial_t\rho_t+\operatorname{div}(\rho_t v_t)=0∂t​ρt​+div(ρt​vt​)=0 gives the weighted Poisson equation in (17). The inverse notation is a shorthand for solving this equation on zero-mean right-hand sides, modulo additive constants.

In general this inversion is still computationally demanding, but special choices of (αt)t(\alpha_t)_t(αt​)t​ lead to simpler formulas; this is the mechanism exploited later by flow matching in Section Generative Models via Flow Matching.

Benamou--Brenier Dynamic Formulation of OT¶

The dynamic formulation identifies W2\Wass_2W2​ with the kinetic energy of the cheapest continuity-equation path. It is the point where OT becomes a least-action principle.

Benamou--Brenier Formulation¶

Instead of assuming that a whole curve (αt)t∈[0,1](\alpha_t)_{t\in[0,1]}(αt​)t∈[0,1]​ is prescribed, one fixes only the endpoints α0\alpha_0α0​ and α1\alpha_1α1​ and minimizes the least-square energy (15). The theorem of Benamou and Brenier states that this geodesic energy is exactly the squared Wasserstein distance Benamou & Brenier, 2000.

Theorem: Benamou--Brenier

For probability measures α0,α1∈P2(Rd)\alpha_0,\alpha_1\in\mathcal P_2(\RR^d)α0​,α1​∈P2​(Rd),

W22(α0,α1)=inf⁡(αt,vt)∫01 ⁣∫Rd∥vt(x)∥2  dαt(x) dt,\Wass_2^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \inf_{(\alpha_t,v_t)} \int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d}\norm{v_t(x)}^2\,\d\alpha_t(x)\d t,W22​(α0​,α1​)=(αt​,vt​)inf​∫01​∫Rd​∥vt​(x)∥2dαt​(x)dt,
(20)

where the infimum is over (αt,vt)(\alpha_t,v_t)(αt​,vt​) solving ∂tαt+∇ ⁣⋅(αtvt)=0\partial_t\alpha_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\alpha_t v_t)=0∂t​αt​+∇⋅(αt​vt​)=0 with αt=0=α0\alpha_{t=0}=\alpha_0αt=0​=α0​ and αt=1=α1\alpha_{t=1}=\alpha_1αt=1​=α1​. If α0\alpha_0α0​ has a density and TTT is the optimal Monge map T♯α0=α1T_\sharp\alpha_0=\alpha_1T♯​α0​=α1​, the minimizer is

αt=((1−t)Id+tT)♯α0,vt((1−t)x+tT(x))=T(x)−x.\alpha_t=((1-t)\Id+tT)_\sharp\alpha_0, \qquad v_t((1-t)x+tT(x))=T(x)-x.αt​=((1−t)Id+tT)♯​α0​,vt​((1−t)x+tT(x))=T(x)−x.
(21)
Proof

For the inequality “dynamic ≤\leq≤ static”, assume first that a Monge map TTT exists and define (αt,vt)(\alpha_t,v_t)(αt​,vt​) by (21). Since the Lagrangian velocity T(x)−xT(x)-xT(x)−x is independent of ttt,

∫01 ⁣∫∥vt∥2  dαt dt=∫∥T(x)−x∥2  dα0(x),\int_0^1\!\int\norm{v_t}^2\,\d\alpha_t\d t = \int\norm{T(x)-x}^2\,\d\alpha_0(x),∫01​∫∥vt​∥2dαt​dt=∫∥T(x)−x∥2dα0​(x),
(22)

so the dynamic cost is no larger than the static Monge cost. Without a Monge map, the same construction uses an optimal coupling π\piπ: sample (X,Y)∼π(X,Y)\sim\pi(X,Y)∼π and move along the straight path γX,Y(t)=(1−t)X+tY\gamma_{X,Y}(t)=(1-t)X+tYγX,Y​(t)=(1−t)X+tY. This path measure has action ∫∥x−y∥2 dπ(x,y)\int\norm{x-y}^2\d\pi(x,y)∫∥x−y∥2dπ(x,y); projecting path velocities onto their conditional mean at time ttt gives an admissible Eulerian velocity with no larger action, so the dynamic value is no larger than the Kantorovich value.

Conversely, for a smooth deterministic path, take the flow TtT_tTt​ defined by T˙t=vt∘Tt\dot T_t=v_t\circ T_tT˙t​=vt​∘Tt​ and T0=IdT_0=\IdT0​=Id. Then αt=(Tt)♯α0\alpha_t=(T_t)_\sharp\alpha_0αt​=(Tt​)♯​α0​ and (T1)♯α0=α1(T_1)_\sharp\alpha_0=\alpha_1(T1​)♯​α0​=α1​. Jensen’s inequality gives

∥T1(x)−x∥2≤∫01∥vt(Tt(x))∥2 dt.\norm{T_1(x)-x}^2 \leq \int_0^1\norm{v_t(T_t(x))}^2\d t.∥T1​(x)−x∥2≤∫01​∥vt​(Tt​(x))∥2dt.
(23)

After integration with respect to α0\alpha_0α0​, the Monge cost is bounded above by the dynamic action. For general finite-energy solutions of the continuity equation, the superposition principle lifts the curve to a probability measure on absolutely continuous paths; applying Jensen’s inequality pathwise gives a coupling of the endpoints whose quadratic cost is no larger than the action. Thus the Kantorovich value is bounded above by the dynamic value.

Convex Moment-Based Reformulation¶

Although (20) is not jointly convex in (αt,vt)(\alpha_t,v_t)(αt​,vt​), it becomes convex after replacing velocities by the momentum measure mt=vtαtm_t=v_t\alpha_tmt​=vt​αt​ and using the perspective action. In the absolutely continuous case αt=ρt  dx\alpha_t=\rho_t\,\d xαt​=ρt​dx and mt(x)=ρt(x)vt(x)m_t(x)=\rho_t(x)v_t(x)mt​(x)=ρt​(x)vt​(x),

W22(α0,α1)=inf⁡∂tρt+div⁡mt=0ρt=0dx=α0, ρt=1dx=α1∫01 ⁣∫Rd∥mt(x)∥2ρt(x) dx  dt,\Wass_2^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \inf_{\substack{\partial_t\rho_t+\operatorname{div}m_t=0\\ \rho_{t=0}\d x=\alpha_0,\ \rho_{t=1}\d x=\alpha_1}} \int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d} \frac{\norm{m_t(x)}^2}{\rho_t(x)} \d x\,\d t,W22​(α0​,α1​)=∂t​ρt​+divmt​=0ρt=0​dx=α0​, ρt=1​dx=α1​​inf​∫01​∫Rd​ρt​(x)∥mt​(x)∥2​dxdt,
(24)

with the usual convention that the integrand is 0 when (ρt,mt)=(0,0)(\rho_t,m_t)=(0,0)(ρt​,mt​)=(0,0) and +∞+\infty+∞ when ρt=0\rho_t=0ρt​=0 but mt≠0m_t\neq0mt​=0. For singular endpoints or curves, the same statement is interpreted with vector-valued momentum measures and the corresponding recession convention. This convex reformulation enables geodesic interpolation by convex optimization once the domain is discretized.

Dual Hamilton--Jacobi Formulation¶

The momentum formulation also has a useful dual. It turns the least-action problem into a Hamilton--Jacobi subsolution inequality for a scalar potential, with equality on the part of space-time actually visited by the optimal curve. With the no-1/21/21/2 convention of (24), the constants are as follows.

Proposition: Dual Benamou--Brenier Problem

Assume, for simplicity, that the densities are smooth, compactly supported, and that boundary terms vanish. Then the convex dynamic value has the dual formulation

W22(α0,α1)=sup⁡ϕ{∫Rdϕ1  dα1−∫Rdϕ0  dα0  :  ∂tϕt+14∥∇ϕt∥2≤0}.\Wass_2^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \sup_{\phi} \left\{ \int_{\RR^d}\phi_1\,\d\alpha_1 - \int_{\RR^d}\phi_0\,\d\alpha_0 \;:\; \partial_t\phi_t+\frac14\norm{\nabla\phi_t}^2\leq 0 \right\}.W22​(α0​,α1​)=ϕsup​{∫Rd​ϕ1​dα1​−∫Rd​ϕ0​dα0​:∂t​ϕt​+41​∥∇ϕt​∥2≤0}.
(25)

If (ρ,m)(\rho,m)(ρ,m) and ϕ\phiϕ are smooth primal and dual optimizers, then

mt=ρt2∇ϕt,∂tϕt+14∥∇ϕt∥2=0on {ρt>0}.m_t=\frac{\rho_t}{2}\nabla\phi_t, \qquad \partial_t\phi_t+\frac14\norm{\nabla\phi_t}^2=0 \quad\text{on }\{\rho_t>0\}.mt​=2ρt​​∇ϕt​,∂t​ϕt​+41​∥∇ϕt​∥2=0on {ρt​>0}.
(26)

Equivalently, the optimal Eulerian velocity is vt=mt/ρt=∇ϕt/2v_t=m_t/\rho_t=\nabla\phi_t/2vt​=mt​/ρt​=∇ϕt​/2.

Proof

Let (ρ,m)(\rho,m)(ρ,m) satisfy the continuity equation and let ϕ\phiϕ be smooth. Multiplying the constraint by ϕ\phiϕ and integrating by parts gives

∫Rdϕ1  dα1−∫Rdϕ0  dα0=∫01 ⁣∫Rd(ρt ∂tϕt+⟨mt,∇ϕt⟩) dx dt.\int_{\RR^d}\phi_1\,\d\alpha_1 - \int_{\RR^d}\phi_0\,\d\alpha_0 = \int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d} \left(\rho_t\,\partial_t\phi_t+\dotp{m_t}{\nabla\phi_t}\right)\d x\d t .∫Rd​ϕ1​dα1​−∫Rd​ϕ0​dα0​=∫01​∫Rd​(ρt​∂t​ϕt​+⟨mt​,∇ϕt​⟩)dxdt.
(27)

If ∂tϕt+∥∇ϕt∥2/4≤0\partial_t\phi_t+\norm{\nabla\phi_t}^2/4\leq0∂t​ϕt​+∥∇ϕt​∥2/4≤0, Young’s inequality yields

ρ ∂tϕ+⟨m,∇ϕ⟩≤−ρ4∥∇ϕ∥2+⟨m,∇ϕ⟩≤∥m∥2ρ,\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\dotp{m}{\nabla\phi} \leq -\frac{\rho}{4}\norm{\nabla\phi}^2+\dotp{m}{\nabla\phi} \leq \frac{\norm m^2}{\rho},ρ∂t​ϕ+⟨m,∇ϕ⟩≤−4ρ​∥∇ϕ∥2+⟨m,∇ϕ⟩≤ρ∥m∥2​,
(28)

with the usual perspective convention. Thus the dual objective of every feasible potential is no larger than the action of every feasible primal pair. Conversely, introducing ϕ\phiϕ as a Lagrange multiplier for ∂tρ+div⁡m=0\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}m=0∂t​ρ+divm=0, and discarding the fixed endpoint contribution, the pointwise minimization contains ∥m∥2/ρ−ρ ∂tϕ−⟨m,∇ϕ⟩\norm m^2/\rho-\rho\,\partial_t\phi-\dotp{m}{\nabla\phi}∥m∥2/ρ−ρ∂t​ϕ−⟨m,∇ϕ⟩. Minimizing over mmm gives m=ρ∇ϕ/2m=\rho\nabla\phi/2m=ρ∇ϕ/2; minimizing over ρ≥0\rho\geq0ρ≥0 is finite exactly under ∂tϕ+∥∇ϕ∥2/4≤0\partial_t\phi+\norm{\nabla\phi}^2/4\leq0∂t​ϕ+∥∇ϕ∥2/4≤0. Fenchel--Rockafellar duality then gives no duality gap in finite-dimensional discretizations. The continuum identity follows by the usual relaxation and approximation, with ϕ\phiϕ interpreted as a Hamilton--Jacobi subsolution. Equality in the two pointwise inequalities gives (26).

This also recovers the static Kantorovich inequality from a dynamic principle. If γ\gammaγ is any smooth curve with γ(0)=x\gamma(0)=xγ(0)=x and γ(1)=y\gamma(1)=yγ(1)=y, then

 d dtϕt(γ(t))=∂tϕt(γ(t))+⟨∇ϕt(γ(t)),γ˙(t)⟩≤∥γ˙(t)∥2.\frac{\d}{\d t}\phi_t(\gamma(t)) = \partial_t\phi_t(\gamma(t))+\dotp{\nabla\phi_t(\gamma(t))}{\dot\gamma(t)} \leq \norm{\dot\gamma(t)}^2.dtd​ϕt​(γ(t))=∂t​ϕt​(γ(t))+⟨∇ϕt​(γ(t)),γ˙​(t)⟩≤∥γ˙​(t)∥2.
(29)

After integration and minimization over curves,

ϕ1(y)−ϕ0(x)≤∥x−y∥2.\phi_1(y)-\phi_0(x)\leq \norm{x-y}^2.ϕ1​(y)−ϕ0​(x)≤∥x−y∥2.
(30)

Thus (ϕ0,ϕ1)(\phi_0,\phi_1)(ϕ0​,ϕ1​) is a feasible static Kantorovich dual pair for the quadratic cost. At optimality the inequality is saturated on the endpoint pairs connected by the primal characteristics.

Proximal Splitting¶

The convex momentum formulation also explains the original Benamou--Brenier solver. After discretization, the ALG2 scheme can be read as a Douglas--Rachford splitting, equivalently ADMM on the Fenchel--Rockafellar dual Papadakis et al., 2014. Suppressing discretization indices, write U=(ρ,m)U=(\rho,m)U=(ρ,m), let F(U)\mathcal F(U)F(U) be the integral of the perspective action, and let G=ιC\mathcal G=\iota_{\mathcal C}G=ιC​ be the indicator of the affine continuity constraint with prescribed endpoints. The problem is min⁡UF(U)+G(U)\min_U \mathcal F(U)+\mathcal G(U)minU​F(U)+G(U).

The two proximal operators separate the nonlinear and linear parts: the prox of F\mathcal FF is local in (t,x)(t,x)(t,x) and amounts to the perspective proximal operator, whereas the prox of G\mathcal GG is the orthogonal projection onto the divergence equation and endpoint constraints. Douglas--Rachford alternates these two simple operations.

Algorithm: Douglas--Rachford for dynamic Benamou--Brenier

Input: Functionals F,G=ιC\mathcal F,\mathcal G=\iota_{\mathcal C}F,G=ιC​, proximal parameter τ>0\tau>0τ>0, initial field Z0Z^0Z0.

Output: Discrete density-momentum field U⋆U^\starU⋆.

For k=0,1,…k=0,1,\ldotsk=0,1,… do:

Uk+1=prox⁡τF(Zk).U^{k+1}=\prox_{\tau\mathcal F}(Z^k).Uk+1=proxτF​(Zk).

Project reflected point: U~k+1=prox⁡τG(2Uk+1−Zk)=Proj⁡C(2Uk+1−Zk).\widetilde U^{k+1} = \prox_{\tau\mathcal G}(2U^{k+1}-Z^k) = \Proj_{\mathcal C}(2U^{k+1}-Z^k).Uk+1=proxτG​(2Uk+1−Zk)=ProjC​(2Uk+1−Zk).

Update Zk+1=Zk+U~k+1−Uk+1.Z^{k+1}=Z^k+\widetilde U^{k+1}-U^{k+1}.Zk+1=Zk+Uk+1−Uk+1.

If ∥Uk+1−U~k+1∥≤tol\norm{U^{k+1}-\widetilde U^{k+1}}\leq\mathrm{tol}∥∥​Uk+1−Uk+1∥∥​≤tol then:

Return Uk+1U^{k+1}Uk+1.

Path-Space Formulation¶

Let S=C([0,1];Rd)\Ss=C([0,1];\RR^d)S=C([0,1];Rd) be the space of continuous paths endowed with the uniform topology. For t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]t∈[0,1] define the evaluation map

Pt:S→Rd,Pt(γ)=γ(t).P_t:\Ss\to\RR^d, \qquad P_t(\gamma)=\gamma(t).Pt​:S→Rd,Pt​(γ)=γ(t).
(31)

The Benamou--Brenier cost admits the equivalent formulation

W22(α0,α1)=inf⁡M∈P(S){∫S ⁣∫01∥γ˙(t)∥2 dt  dM(γ)  :  (P0)♯M=α0, (P1)♯M=α1}.\Wass_2^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \inf_{M\in\Pp(\Ss)} \enscond{ \int_{\Ss}\!\int_0^1\norm{\dot\gamma(t)}^2\d t\,\d M(\gamma) }{ (P_0)_\sharp M=\alpha_0,\ (P_1)_\sharp M=\alpha_1 }.W22​(α0​,α1​)=M∈P(S)inf​{∫S​∫01​∥γ˙​(t)∥2dtdM(γ):(P0​)♯​M=α0​, (P1​)♯​M=α1​}.
(32)

If α0\alpha_0α0​ has a density, the minimizer M∗M^*M∗ is unique. Its time marginals reproduce the optimal curve: αt=(Pt)♯M∗\alpha_t=(P_t)_\sharp M^*αt​=(Pt​)♯​M∗ for all ttt. Furthermore, for a.e. ttt, denoting Qt(γ)=γ˙(t)Q_t(\gamma)=\dot\gamma(t)Qt​(γ)=γ˙​(t) on absolutely continuous paths, the conditional law of the velocity is deterministic:

(Pt,Qt)♯M∗( dx, dq)=αt( dx)δvt∗(x)( dq),(P_t,Q_t)_\sharp M^*(\d x,\d q) = \alpha_t(\d x)\delta_{v_t^*(x)}(\d q),(Pt​,Qt​)♯​M∗(dx,dq)=αt​(dx)δvt∗​(x)​(dq),
(33)

where vt∗v_t^*vt∗​ is the optimal velocity field in the Benamou--Brenier formulation. Hence M∗M^*M∗ concentrates on straight-line geodesics and, for a.e. ttt, assigns exactly one direction at αt\alpha_tαt​-a.e. spatial point.

Generalized Dynamic Wasserstein Distances¶

The quadratic Benamou--Brenier formula is only one instance of a broader fixed-mass dynamic language. The goal of this section is to define a large family of geodesic-like distances on spaces of probability measures by modifying the action minimized in the Benamou--Brenier formula. The objects introduced here are metric: they specify admissible curves, tangent variables and path energies. All descent constructions are postponed to Generalized Dynamic Wasserstein Flows, where these distances are used to generate gradient-flow PDE models.

In the mass-preserving Euclidean setting, the basic input is an instantaneous action A(α,w)\mathbb A(\alpha,w)A(α,w), where α\alphaα is the current measure and www is an admissible velocity representative. When this action is normalized as a squared infinitesimal speed, it generates the length-space value

DA2(α0,α1)=inf⁡αt,vt{∫01A(αt,vt)  dt:∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0, αt=0=α0, αt=1=α1}.\mathsf D_{\mathbb A}^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \inf_{\alpha_t,v_t} \left\{ \int_0^1 \mathbb A(\alpha_t,v_t)\,\d t : \partial_t\alpha_t+\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)=0, \ \alpha_{t=0}=\alpha_0, \ \alpha_{t=1}=\alpha_1 \right\}.DA2​(α0​,α1​)=αt​,vt​inf​{∫01​A(αt​,vt​)dt:∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0, αt=0​=α0​, αt=1​=α1​}.
(34)

Equivalently, one may quotient by velocity fields that induce the same first-order variation of the measure. The formula above should be read as a dynamic definition of the distance, not as a property automatically satisfied by an arbitrary discrepancy. Some standard distances, such as Wp\Wass_pWp​, are first written with a ppp-homogeneous action and then squared by taking a constant-speed parametrization; this normalization is made explicit below. Different choices of A\mathbb AA change the resulting geometry; Generalized Dynamic Wasserstein Flows later reuses these choices when dynamics are introduced.

Quadratic, or Riemannian, Tangent Actions¶

A particularly transparent case occurs when w↦A(α,w)w\mapsto\mathbb A(\alpha,w)w↦A(α,w) is quadratic. For simplicity, take admissible velocities in L2(α;Rd)L^2(\alpha;\RR^d)L2(α;Rd); in some applications this Hilbert space is replaced by a closed subspace encoding additional constraints. If the polarization of A\mathbb AA is represented by a positive self-adjoint operator Qα:L2(α;Rd)→L2(α;Rd)Q_\alpha:L^2(\alpha;\RR^d)\to L^2(\alpha;\RR^d)Qα​:L2(α;Rd)→L2(α;Rd),

A(α;w,z)=⟨Qαw,z⟩L2(α),A(α,w)=⟨Qαw,w⟩L2(α),\mathbb A(\alpha;w,z) = \left\langle Q_\alpha w,z\right\rangle_{L^2(\alpha)}, \qquad \mathbb A(\alpha,w)=\left\langle Q_\alpha w,w\right\rangle_{L^2(\alpha)},A(α;w,z)=⟨Qα​w,z⟩L2(α)​,A(α,w)=⟨Qα​w,w⟩L2(α)​,
(35)

then the least-action distance generated by this tensor is

DQ2(α0,α1)=DA2(α0,α1)=inf⁡∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0αt=0=α0, αt=1=α1∫01⟨Qαtvt,vt⟩L2(αt) dt.\mathsf D_Q^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \mathsf D_{\mathbb A}^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \inf_{\substack{\partial_t\alpha_t+\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)=0\\ \alpha_{t=0}=\alpha_0,\ \alpha_{t=1}=\alpha_1}} \int_0^1 \left\langle Q_{\alpha_t}v_t,v_t\right\rangle_{L^2(\alpha_t)} \d t .DQ2​(α0​,α1​)=DA2​(α0​,α1​)=∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0αt=0​=α0​, αt=1​=α1​​inf​∫01​⟨Qαt​​vt​,vt​⟩L2(αt​)​dt.
(36)

The usual W2\Wass_2W2​ geometry corresponds to Qα=IdQ_\alpha=\IdQα​=Id in this simplified notation. Thus QαQ_\alphaQα​ records how the chosen geometry deforms the Euclidean L2(α)L^2(\alpha)L2(α) tangent norm: no deformation for W2\Wass_2W2​, and a nontrivial tensor for generalized Riemannian geometries. Generalized Dynamic Wasserstein Flows later reuses the same tensor as a preconditioner for metric descent.

Local Velocity Actions¶

Many dynamic distances are local with respect to a reference measure λ\lambdaλ. Write α=aλ\alpha=a\lambdaα=aλ. A velocity action is specified by a pointwise integrand

A:[0,+∞)×Rd→[0,+∞],(a,w)↦A(a,w),A:[0,+\infty)\times\RR^d\to[0,+\infty], \qquad (a,w)\mapsto A(a,w),A:[0,+∞)×Rd→[0,+∞],(a,w)↦A(a,w),
(37)

where a∈R+a\in\RR_+a∈R+​ is a density value and w∈Rdw\in\RR^dw∈Rd is a velocity value, and defines

A(α,w)=∫A( dα dλ(x),w(x)) dλ(x).\mathbb A(\alpha,w) = \int A\left(\frac{\d\alpha}{\d\lambda}(x),w(x)\right)\d\lambda(x).A(α,w)=∫A(dλdα​(x),w(x))dλ(x).
(38)

For a fixed reference λ\lambdaλ, this covers density-dependent mobilities and congestion constraints. If, in addition, AAA is positively 1-homogeneous in its first variable, A(ηa,w)=ηA(a,w)A(\eta a,w)=\eta A(a,w)A(ηa,w)=ηA(a,w) for η≥0\eta\geq0η≥0, then the same formula is intrinsic: replacing λ\lambdaλ by another dominating measure gives the same value. The usual Benamou--Brenier action is the model case

A2(a,w)=a∥w∥2,A(α,w)=∫∥w∥2 dα.A_2(a,w)=a\norm{w}^2, \qquad \mathbb A(\alpha,w)=\int\norm{w}^2\d\alpha .A2​(a,w)=a∥w∥2,A(α,w)=∫∥w∥2dα.
(39)

Homogeneous Momentum Actions¶

The same action can be written in momentum variables, and this is the form in which convexity and metric properties are easiest to read. Set μ=αw\mu=\alpha wμ=αw, so that μ\muμ is a vector-valued measure. When the local description is written with the same reference λ\lambdaλ, so that α=aλ\alpha=a\lambdaα=aλ and μ=mλ\mu=m\lambdaμ=mλ, the pointwise momentum perspective is

JA(a,m):={A(a,m/a),a>0,0,a=0 and m=0,+∞,a=0 and m≠0,J_A(a,m) \eqdef \begin{cases} A(a,m/a), & a>0,\\ 0, & a=0\ \text{and}\ m=0,\\ +\infty, & a=0\ \text{and}\ m\neq0, \end{cases}JA​(a,m):=⎩⎨⎧​A(a,m/a),0,+∞,​a>0,a=0 and m=0,a=0 and m=0,​

JA,λ(α,μ):=∫JA ⁣( dα dλ, dμ dλ) dλ,\mathbb J_{A,\lambda}(\alpha,\mu) \eqdef \int J_A\!\left( \frac{\d\alpha}{\d\lambda}, \frac{\d\mu}{\d\lambda} \right)\d\lambda,JA,λ​(α,μ):=∫JA​(dλdα​,dλdμ​)dλ,

with value +∞+\infty+∞ if α\alphaα or the total variation ∣μ∣|\mu|∣μ∣ is not absolutely continuous with respect to λ\lambdaλ. This zero-density convention is the lower-semicontinuous one for the superlinear actions used below; other growths use the corresponding recession extension. If AAA is positively 1-homogeneous in aaa, then JAJ_AJA​ is jointly 1-homogeneous: JA(ηa,ηm)=ηJA(a,m)J_A(\eta a,\eta m)=\eta J_A(a,m)JA​(ηa,ηm)=ηJA​(a,m). In that intrinsic case the value of JA,λ\mathbb J_{A,\lambda}JA,λ​ is independent of the dominating reference measure, and we write simply JA\mathbb J_AJA​. For A2(a,w)=a∥w∥2A_2(a,w)=a\norm{w}^2A2​(a,w)=a∥w∥2, one recovers the quadratic perspective

J2(a,m)=∥m∥2a,J_2(a,m)=\frac{\norm m^2}{a},J2​(a,m)=a∥m∥2​,

which is the integrand used in the convex Benamou--Brenier formulation.

Fix a reference measure λ\lambdaλ, omitted from the notation only in the intrinsic case where JA,λ\mathbb J_{A,\lambda}JA,λ​ does not depend on λ\lambdaλ. Zero self-distance is obtained by the constant curve. Without homogeneity or nondegeneracy, the same momentum action remains useful as a variational principle, but its rrr-th root need not define a distance.

Example: Wasserstein-ppp action

The usual Wp\Wass_pWp​ distances correspond to changing only the homogeneity of the Benamou--Brenier action. The specific objects to insert in the general framework are

Ap(a,w)=a∥w∥p,Jp(a,m)={∥m∥p/ap−1,a>0,0,(a,m)=(0,0),+∞,a=0, m≠0,A_p(a,w)=a\norm{w}^p, \qquad J_p(a,m)= \begin{cases} \norm{m}^p/a^{p-1}, & a>0,\\ 0, & (a,m)=(0,0),\\ +\infty, & a=0,\ m\neq0, \end{cases}Ap​(a,w)=a∥w∥p,Jp​(a,m)=⎩⎨⎧​∥m∥p/ap−1,0,+∞,​a>0,(a,m)=(0,0),a=0, m=0,​
(49)

With A=ApA=A_pA=Ap​, Proposition Proposition: Homogeneous Dynamic Actions Define Distances gives the usual identity DAp=Wp\mathsf D_{A_p}=\Wass_pDAp​​=Wp​. The corresponding squared length-space normalization is

Ap(α,w)=(∫∥w∥p dα)2/p.\mathbb A_p(\alpha,w) = \left(\int\norm{w}^p\d\alpha\right)^{2/p}.Ap​(α,w)=(∫∥w∥pdα)2/p.

Concave-Mobility Actions¶

One can instead keep a quadratic momentum action and change the mobility. Dolbeault, Nazaret and Savaré introduced this construction as a class of generalized transport distances adapted to nonlinear diffusion Dolbeault et al., 2009. Let I⊂[0,+∞)I\subset[0,+\infty)I⊂[0,+∞) be a convex interval and let θ:I→[0,+∞)\theta:I\to[0,+\infty)θ:I→[0,+∞) be concave. Define

Jθ(a,m):={∥m∥2/θ(a),θ(a)>0,0,θ(a)=0 and m=0,+∞,θ(a)=0 and m≠0.J_\theta(a,m) \eqdef \begin{cases} \norm{m}^2/\theta(a), & \theta(a)>0,\\ 0, & \theta(a)=0 \text{ and } m=0,\\ +\infty, & \theta(a)=0 \text{ and } m\neq0. \end{cases}Jθ​(a,m):=⎩⎨⎧​∥m∥2/θ(a),0,+∞,​θ(a)>0,θ(a)=0 and m=0,θ(a)=0 and m=0.​

The corresponding velocity action is

Aθ(a,w)=Jθ(a,aw)=a2∥w∥2θ(a).A_\theta(a,w)=J_\theta(a,aw)=\frac{a^2\norm{w}^2}{\theta(a)}.Aθ​(a,w)=Jθ​(a,aw)=θ(a)a2∥w∥2​.

This is why concavity of the mobility, rather than convexity, is the structural condition that makes the continuity-equation formulation convex.

Fix now a reference measure λ\lambdaλ. If α=aλ\alpha=a\lambdaα=aλ, the induced squared tangent action is

and it is set to +∞+\infty+∞ when α≪̸λ\alpha\not\ll\lambdaα≪λ. Equivalently, on the set where θ(a(x))>0\theta(a(x))>0θ(a(x))>0,

Dynamic Spectral Wasserstein Distances¶

The static spectral distances of Spectral and Robust Wasserstein Distances penalize a coupling through the covariance of its displacement. A dynamic version keeps the continuity equation but replaces the pointwise kinetic energy by a gauge of the whole velocity covariance. The resulting action is nonlocal in space: velocity directions are charged globally through their covariance, rather than independently at each point.

Let γ\gammaγ be a monotone spectral gauge on S+d\mathbb S_+^dS+d​. For a probability measure α\alphaα and a velocity field v∈L2(α;Rd)v\in L^2(\alpha;\RR^d)v∈L2(α;Rd), define the spectral tangent action

Aγ(α,v):=γ ⁣(∫v(x)v(x)⊤ dα(x)).\mathbb A_\gamma(\alpha,v) \eqdef \gamma\!\left(\int v(x)v(x)^\top\d\alpha(x)\right).Aγ​(α,v):=γ(∫v(x)v(x)⊤dα(x)).
(58)

The trace gauge gives the usual Wasserstein tangent action, while the operator gauge γ(M)=λmax⁡(M)\gamma(M)=\lambda_{\max}(M)γ(M)=λmax​(M) charges only the largest directional velocity variance. With the length-distance notation introduced in (34), the associated dynamic action distance is

Wγ,dyn2:=DAγ2.\mathsf W_{\gamma,\mathrm{dyn}}^2 \eqdef \mathsf D_{\mathbb A_\gamma}^2 .Wγ,dyn2​:=DAγ​2​.
(59)

In density--momentum variables, this corresponds to the measure action

Jγ(α,μ)=γ ⁣(∫( dμ dα)( dμ dα)⊤ dα),\mathbb J_\gamma(\alpha,\mu) = \gamma\!\left(\int \left(\frac{\d\mu}{\d\alpha}\right) \left(\frac{\d\mu}{\d\alpha}\right)^\top \d\alpha\right),Jγ​(α,μ)=γ(∫(dαdμ​)(dαdμ​)⊤dα),
(60)

or, when α=ρ  dx\alpha=\rho\,\d xα=ρdx and μ=m  dx\mu=m\,\d xμ=mdx,

Jγ(ρ,m)=γ ⁣(∫m(x)m(x)⊤ρ(x)  dx).\mathbb J_\gamma(\rho,m) = \gamma\!\left(\int \frac{m(x)m(x)^\top}{\rho(x)}\,\d x\right).Jγ​(ρ,m)=γ(∫ρ(x)m(x)m(x)⊤​dx).
(61)

This functional is convex in the density--momentum fields (ρ,m)(\rho,m)(ρ,m) by the matrix perspective, together with the monotonicity and convexity of γ\gammaγ. It is nevertheless not, in general, obtained by integrating a pointwise action density, because the covariance is computed globally before applying γ\gammaγ. It becomes local only for linear spectral gauges. For instance, if γ(M)=tr⁡(GM)\gamma(M)=\operatorname{tr}(GM)γ(M)=tr(GM) with G⪰0G\succeq0G⪰0, then the velocity and momentum densities are

Alin(a,w)=a w⊤Gw,Jlin(a,m)=m⊤Gma,A_{\mathrm{lin}}(a,w)=a\,w^\top G w, \qquad J_{\mathrm{lin}}(a,m)=\frac{m^\top G m}{a},Alin​(a,w)=aw⊤Gw,Jlin​(a,m)=am⊤Gm​,
(62)

and the trace gauge, G=IdG=\IdG=Id in γ(M)=tr⁡(GM)\gamma(M)=\operatorname{tr}(GM)γ(M)=tr(GM), recovers the usual Benamou--Brenier action.

The following result, in the form used for normalized spectral flows in Peyré, 2026, shows that this dynamic construction is not merely infinitesimal: it exactly recovers the static displacement-covariance formulation.

Let γ\gammaγ be a monotone spectral gauge and let α0,α1∈P2(Rd)\alpha_0,\alpha_1\in\mathcal P_2(\RR^d)α0​,α1​∈P2​(Rd). Then

Wγ,dyn2(α0,α1)=Wγ2(α0,α1).\mathsf W_{\gamma,\mathrm{dyn}}^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \Wass_\gamma^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1).Wγ,dyn2​(α0​,α1​)=Wγ2​(α0​,α1​).

The use of this geometry for normalized flows, including the operator-gauge connection with Muon-type normalization, is developed in Dynamic Spectral Wasserstein Flows.

Kernelized Benamou--Brenier Distances¶

A different way to deform the Benamou--Brenier geometry is to keep the local continuity equation but to measure velocities in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space rather than in L2(α)L^2(\alpha)L2(α). This construction is motivated by Stein variational gradient descent, studied later in Stein Variational Gradient Descent: the kernel makes the velocity field smooth and computable from particles, at the price of defining a much more restrictive transport geometry.

Let kkk be a positive definite kernel on Rd\RR^dRd with scalar RKHS Hk\RKHS_kHk​. The vector-valued RKHS is

Hkd:=Hk×⋯×Hk,∥v∥Hkd2:=∑ℓ=1d∥vℓ∥Hk2.\RKHS_k^d\eqdef \RKHS_k\times\cdots\times\RKHS_k, \qquad \norm{v}_{\RKHS_k^d}^2 \eqdef \sum_{\ell=1}^d\norm{v_\ell}_{\RKHS_k}^2.Hkd​:=Hk​×⋯×Hk​,∥v∥Hkd​2​:=ℓ=1∑d​∥vℓ​∥Hk​2​.
(67)

This is the vector-valued analogue of the scalar RKHS norm used for MMDs in Dual RKHS Norms and Maximum Mean Discrepancies. The specific kernelized tangent action is

Ak(α,v):=∥v∥Hkd2,Wk2:=DAk2,\mathbb A_k(\alpha,v) \eqdef \norm{v}_{\RKHS_k^d}^2, \qquad \mathcal W_k^2 \eqdef \mathsf D_{\mathbb A_k}^2,Ak​(α,v):=∥v∥Hkd​2​,Wk2​:=DAk​2​,
(68)

where the general distance formula (34) is understood with the restricted admissible tangent class vt∈Hkdv_t\in\RKHS_k^dvt​∈Hkd​. The action itself is independent of α\alphaα; the measure only enters through the continuity equation ∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0\partial_t\alpha_t+\diverg(\alpha_t v_t)=0∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0, which says how the common smooth velocity field moves all particles. This type of Stein geometry was introduced in the analysis of SVGD by Liu and Wang Liu & Wang, 2016Liu, 2017 and later developed geometrically in Duncan et al., 2019Nüsken & Renger, 2021. The important caveat is that the admissible tangent space is the smooth RKHS class, not the whole Wasserstein tangent space.

Proposition: Kernelized Dynamic Distance

The quantity Wk\mathcal W_kWk​ defined by (68) is an extended distance on each finite-action component of probability measures. More precisely, it is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and Wk(α0,α1)=0\mathcal W_k(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)=0Wk​(α0​,α1​)=0 implies α0=α1\alpha_0=\alpha_1α0​=α1​. It can take the value +∞+\infty+∞ between different components.

Proof

This is the standard length-space argument for a quadratic action. The constant curve gives zero self-distance. If Wk(α0,α1)=0\mathcal W_k(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)=0Wk​(α0​,α1​)=0, a zero-action relaxed curve has vt=0v_t=0vt​=0 for a.e. ttt, hence the continuity equation gives ∂tαt=0\partial_t\alpha_t=0∂t​αt​=0 and α0=α1\alpha_0=\alpha_1α0​=α1​. Symmetry follows by time reversal and by replacing vtv_tvt​ with −v1−t-v_{1-t}−v1−t​. For the triangle inequality, concatenate two almost optimal curves of actions E1E_1E1​ and E2E_2E2​. Compressing the first into a time interval of length τ\tauτ multiplies its action by 1/τ1/\tau1/τ, and compressing the second into length 1−τ1-\tau1−τ multiplies its action by 1/(1−τ)1/(1-\tau)1/(1−τ). Optimizing over τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1)τ∈(0,1) gives (E1+E2)2(\sqrt{E_1}+\sqrt{E_2})^2(E1​​+E2​​)2, and taking infima yields the triangle inequality.

One should read Wk\mathcal W_kWk​ as an extended distance on finite-action components, not as a replacement for W2\Wass_2W2​ on all of P2(Rd)\Pp_2(\RR^d)P2​(Rd). A useful sufficient condition for finiteness is that the endpoints lie on the same RKHS-flow orbit: if there exists v∈L2([0,1];Hkd)v\in L^2([0,1];\RKHS_k^d)v∈L2([0,1];Hkd​) whose flow map Φt\Phi_tΦt​ solves Φ˙t=vt∘Φt\dot\Phi_t=v_t\circ\Phi_tΦ˙t​=vt​∘Φt​ and satisfies α1=(Φ1)♯α0\alpha_1=(\Phi_1)_\sharp\alpha_0α1​=(Φ1​)♯​α0​, then Wk2(α0,α1)≤∫01∥vt∥Hkd2 dt\mathcal W_k^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)\leq\int_0^1\norm{v_t}_{\RKHS_k^d}^2\d tWk2​(α0​,α1​)≤∫01​∥vt​∥Hkd​2​dt. In particular, for strictly positive definite kernels, two discrete measures with the same weights and distinct moving support points are at finite distance whenever their atoms can be connected by noncolliding smooth paths, because RKHS interpolation constructs vector fields realizing the prescribed atom velocities along the paths.

The same condition also explains the limitation. If kkk is smooth enough that Hkd\RKHS_k^dHkd​ embeds into Lipschitz vector fields, finite-action curves are induced by regular flows. Atomic measures remain atomic with the same number of atoms, so a Dirac mass cannot be transported at finite kernelized action to a measure with a density. This lack of splitting is precisely what makes the geometry useful for deterministic particle methods, and also what makes it a nontrivial extended object rather than a full probability metric.

Nonlocal Wasserstein Distances¶

The local dynamic distances above transport mass through a vector field on the base space and a classical continuity equation. Nonlocal geometries use a different tangent model: the elementary motion is an exchange across an edge or a jump from xxx to yyy. The common data are a reversible kernel KKK, a symmetric edge or jump measure J\mathsf JJ, a pairwise increment ∇ˉ\bar\nabla∇ˉ, and a pair-space action AK\mathbb A_KAK​. The tangent variable is therefore attached to pairs of points, not to a single point xxx, so these constructions are not simply obtained by choosing another pointwise local action-density A(ρ(x),m(x))A(\rho(x),m(x))A(ρ(x),m(x)).

There are two complementary versions. On a finite state space, the goal is to put a Wasserstein-like geometry on the probability simplex so that the entropy gradient flow is exactly a prescribed reversible Markov chain Maas, 2011Mielke, 2013Chow et al., 2012. On a continuum space, the same edge calculus becomes a jump calculus over X×X\mathcal X\times\mathcal XX×X, which models nonlocal motion, heavy-tailed jumps, and fractional-type diffusion; this is the construction of Erbar Erbar, 2012, building on nonlinear mobilities Dolbeault et al., 2009, with subsequent metric and asymptotic refinements Slepčev & Warren, 2022.

In both settings the canonical mobility for entropy is the logarithmic mean

θ(a,b):={a−blog⁡a−log⁡b,a≠b,a,a=b,\theta(a,b)\eqdef \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{a-b}{\log a-\log b}, & a\neq b,\\[.4em] a, & a=b, \end{cases}θ(a,b):=⎩⎨⎧​loga−logba−b​,a,​a=b,a=b,​
(69)

with the usual lower-semicontinuous extension at a=0a=0a=0 or b=0b=0b=0. It appears because θ(a,b)(log⁡a−log⁡b)=a−b\theta(a,b)(\log a-\log b)=a-bθ(a,b)(loga−logb)=a−b, which is the edge-wise chain rule identifying entropy-driven flows with the underlying reversible Markov or jump dynamics.

Continuum Jump Kernels¶

The continuum version replaces graph edges by a symmetric measure on pairs. Its action is still quadratic, but the tangent variable is an antisymmetric jump velocity v(x,y)v(x,y)v(x,y), and the mobility depends simultaneously on the two endpoint densities ρ(x)\rho(x)ρ(x) and ρ(y)\rho(y)ρ(y). It is best viewed as a convex action on the pair space X×X\mathcal X\times\mathcal XX×X, rather than as an integral of independent costs attached to single base points xxx.

Let (X,m)(\mathcal X,\mathfrak m)(X,m) be a reference measure space, and let K(x,⋅)K(x,\cdot)K(x,⋅) be a nonnegative measure on X\mathcal XX for each x∈Xx\in\mathcal Xx∈X, possibly of infinite total mass. We write this kernel as K(x, dy)K(x,\d y)K(x,dy) to emphasize that the integration variable is yyy. The pair measure J\mathsf JJ on X×X\mathcal X\times\mathcal XX×X is defined by testing against nonnegative measurable functions Φ\PhiΦ:

∫X×XΦ(x,y) J( dx, dy):=∫X(∫XΦ(x,y) K(x, dy))m( dx).\int_{\mathcal X\times\mathcal X}\Phi(x,y)\,\mathsf J(\d x,\d y) \eqdef \int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathcal X}\Phi(x,y)\,K(x,\d y)\right)\mathfrak m(\d x).∫X×X​Φ(x,y)J(dx,dy):=∫X​(∫X​Φ(x,y)K(x,dy))m(dx).
(70)

The reversibility assumption is precisely that this measure J\mathsf JJ is symmetric, i.e. invariant under (x,y)↦(y,x)(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)(x,y)↦(y,x). For a density ρ= dα/ dm\rho=\d\alpha/\d\mathfrak mρ=dα/dm, write

∇ˉφ(x,y):=φ(y)−φ(x)\bar\nabla \varphi(x,y)\eqdef \varphi(y)-\varphi(x)∇ˉφ(x,y):=φ(y)−φ(x)
(71)

for the nonlocal gradient, and use the logarithmic mean θ\thetaθ defined in (69). A curve αt=ρtm\alpha_t=\rho_t\mathfrak mαt​=ρt​m driven by an antisymmetric velocity vt(x,y)=−vt(y,x)v_t(x,y)=-v_t(y,x)vt​(x,y)=−vt​(y,x) satisfies the nonlocal continuity equation if, for all test functions φ\varphiφ,

 d dt∫φ  dαt=12∬∇ˉφ(x,y) vt(x,y) θ(ρt(x),ρt(y)) J( dx, dy).\frac{\d}{\d t}\int \varphi\,\d\alpha_t = \frac12 \iint \bar\nabla\varphi(x,y)\, v_t(x,y)\, \theta(\rho_t(x),\rho_t(y))\, \mathsf J(\d x,\d y).dtd​∫φdαt​=21​∬∇ˉφ(x,y)vt​(x,y)θ(ρt​(x),ρt​(y))J(dx,dy).
(72)

The corresponding pair-space tangent action is

Proposition: Metric Properties of Nonlocal Transport

Under the regularity and irreducibility assumptions of Erbar (2012), WK\mathcal W_KWK​ is an extended distance on the set of probability measures absolutely continuous with respect to m\mathfrak mm, and finite-distance pairs are connected by constant-speed geodesics.

Proof

We use the analytic compactness and lower-semicontinuity theorem of Erbar (2012) for the logarithmic-mean action. Namely, action-bounded sequences of admissible curves are compact for the narrow topology, the weak nonlocal continuity equation is closed under this convergence, and the action is lower semicontinuous.

Nonnegativity is immediate from the definition of AK(α,v)\mathbb A_K(\alpha,v)AK​(α,v). If α0=α1\alpha_0=\alpha_1α0​=α1​, the constant curve ρt=ρ0\rho_t=\rho_0ρt​=ρ0​, vt=0v_t=0vt​=0, is admissible and has zero action.

Symmetry follows by time reversal. If (ρt,vt)(\rho_t,v_t)(ρt​,vt​) transports α0\alpha_0α0​ to α1\alpha_1α1​, set ρ~t=ρ1−t\tilde\rho_t=\rho_{1-t}ρ~​t​=ρ1−t​ and v~t=−v1−t\tilde v_t=-v_{1-t}v~t​=−v1−t​. The weak continuity equation is preserved by this change of time, and the quadratic action is unchanged. Thus WK(α0,α1)=WK(α1,α0)\mathcal W_K(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)=\mathcal W_K(\alpha_1,\alpha_0)WK​(α0​,α1​)=WK​(α1​,α0​).

For the triangle inequality, let (ρt0,vt0)(\rho^0_t,v^0_t)(ρt0​,vt0​) connect α0\alpha_0α0​ to α1\alpha_1α1​ with action A0A_0A0​, and let (ρt1,vt1)(\rho^1_t,v^1_t)(ρt1​,vt1​) connect α1\alpha_1α1​ to α2\alpha_2α2​ with action A1A_1A1​. For 0<ζ<10<\zeta<10<ζ<1, concatenate the two curves by

(ρt,vt)={(ρt/ζ0, ζ−1vt/ζ0),0≤t≤ζ,(ρ(t−ζ)/(1−ζ)1, (1−ζ)−1v(t−ζ)/(1−ζ)1),ζ<t≤1.(\rho_t,v_t)= \begin{cases} \bigl(\rho^0_{t/\zeta},\,\zeta^{-1}v^0_{t/\zeta}\bigr), &0\leq t\leq\zeta,\\[.35em] \bigl(\rho^1_{(t-\zeta)/(1-\zeta)},\,(1-\zeta)^{-1}v^1_{(t-\zeta)/(1-\zeta)}\bigr), &\zeta<t\leq1. \end{cases}(ρt​,vt​)={(ρt/ζ0​,ζ−1vt/ζ0​),(ρ(t−ζ)/(1−ζ)1​,(1−ζ)−1v(t−ζ)/(1−ζ)1​),​0≤t≤ζ,ζ<t≤1.​
(75)

The velocity factors are exactly those required by the weak continuity equation after time rescaling. Since v↦AK(α,v)v\mapsto\mathbb A_K(\alpha,v)v↦AK​(α,v) is quadratic, the concatenated action is

A0ζ+A11−ζ.\frac{A_0}{\zeta}+\frac{A_1}{1-\zeta}.ζA0​​+1−ζA1​​.
(76)

Optimizing in ζ\zetaζ, for instance taking ζ=A0/(A0+A1)\zeta=\sqrt{A_0}/(\sqrt{A_0}+\sqrt{A_1})ζ=A0​​/(A0​​+A1​​) when both actions are positive, gives the action (A0+A1)2(\sqrt{A_0}+\sqrt{A_1})^2(A0​​+A1​​)2. Taking infima over the two curves proves the triangle inequality.

If WK(α0,α1)=0\mathcal W_K(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)=0WK​(α0​,α1​)=0, choose admissible curves with actions tending to zero. Compactness and lower semicontinuity give a limiting admissible curve of zero action. Hence vt=0v_t=0vt​=0 for θ(ρt(x),ρt(y))J( dx, dy) dt\theta(\rho_t(x),\rho_t(y))\mathsf J(\d x,\d y)\d tθ(ρt​(x),ρt​(y))J(dx,dy)dt-a.e. (t,x,y)(t,x,y)(t,x,y), and the weak continuity equation gives

for every admissible test function φ\varphiφ. The irreducibility/separation assumption in Erbar (2012) ensures that these test functions determine the measure, so αt\alpha_tαt​ is constant and α0=α1\alpha_0=\alpha_1α0​=α1​.

Finally, if WK(α0,α1)<+∞\mathcal W_K(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)<+\inftyWK​(α0​,α1​)<+∞, the same direct-method compactness applied to a minimizing sequence gives a minimizer. Reparametrizing this minimizing curve by metric arclength gives a constant-speed curve; after this parametrization,

The consequences for entropy dynamics and fractional PDE examples are developed in the nonlocal Wasserstein-flow section below.

Discrete Wasserstein Distances on Markov Chains¶

The finite-state version keeps the same pair-space philosophy, but with a finite graph of admissible exchanges. It is not the naive Euclidean metric on the simplex. The key idea, introduced by Maas and independently developed in related forms by Mielke and by Chow--Huang--Li--Zhou, is to use the transition graph of a reversible Markov chain to define both the admissible directions and the mobility of the mass Maas, 2011Mielke, 2013Chow et al., 2012. The entropy gradient-flow interpretation is stated later in Proposition: Entropy Gradient Flow of a Reversible Markov Chain.

Let X={1,…,n}\mathcal X=\{1,\ldots,n\}X={1,…,n} and let K=(Kij)K=(K_{ij})K=(Kij​) denote the off-diagonal transition rates of an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain reversible with respect to a probability vector π\piπ, so that πiKij=πjKji\pi_iK_{ij}=\pi_jK_{ji}πi​Kij​=πj​Kji​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j. Write

Jij:=πiKij=πjKji\mathsf J_{ij}\eqdef \pi_iK_{ij}=\pi_jK_{ji}Jij​:=πi​Kij​=πj​Kji​
(79)

for the symmetric edge measure, the finite counterpart of the jump measure used above. The transported object is a mass histogram

Σn:={a∈R+n:∑iai=1}.\Sigma_n\eqdef\left\{a\in\RR_+^n:\sum_i a_i=1\right\}.Σn​:={a∈R+n​:i∑​ai​=1}.
(80)

Relative densities only enter as auxiliary variables with respect to the invariant law:

ρi(a):=aiπi,ai=πiρi(a).\rho_i(a)\eqdef \frac{a_i}{\pi_i}, \qquad a_i=\pi_i\rho_i(a).ρi​(a):=πi​ai​​,ai​=πi​ρi​(a).
(81)

The logarithmic mean θ\thetaθ defined in (69) is the mobility selected so that the entropy calculus later recovers exactly the Markov evolution. The identity θ(a,b)(log⁡a−log⁡b)=a−b\theta(a,b)(\log a-\log b)=a-bθ(a,b)(loga−logb)=a−b converts entropy gradients into density differences along graph edges. For a potential ψ∈Rn\psi\in\RR^nψ∈Rn, set

∇ˉψ(i,j):=ψj−ψi.\bar\nabla\psi(i,j)\eqdef\psi_j-\psi_i.∇ˉψ(i,j):=ψj​−ψi​.
(82)

The finite nonlocal divergence is encoded by the density Onsager operator and by its mass form

(Kρψ)i:=∑jKijθ(ρi,ρj)(ψi−ψj),(Laψ)i:=πi(Kρ(a)ψ)i.(\mathcal K_\rho\psi)_i \eqdef \sum_j K_{ij}\theta(\rho_i,\rho_j)(\psi_i-\psi_j), \qquad (\mathcal L_a\psi)_i \eqdef \pi_i(\mathcal K_{\rho(a)}\psi)_i.(Kρ​ψ)i​:=j∑​Kij​θ(ρi​,ρj​)(ψi​−ψj​),(La​ψ)i​:=πi​(Kρ(a)​ψ)i​.
(83)

with tangent action

AK(a,ψ):=12∑i,jJijθ(ρi(a),ρj(a))(∇ˉψ(i,j))2.\mathbb A_K(a,\psi) \eqdef \frac12\sum_{i,j}\mathsf J_{ij}\theta(\rho_i(a),\rho_j(a)) (\bar\nabla\psi(i,j))^2.AK​(a,ψ):=21​i,j∑​Jij​θ(ρi​(a),ρj​(a))(∇ˉψ(i,j))2.
(84)

This is the finite-state squared tangent action; the tangent variable is the potential ψ\psiψ, or equivalently the induced edge flux, rather than an ambient Euclidean vector field.

The discrete transport distance is

WK2(a0,a1):=inf⁡at,ψt∫01AK(at,ψt)  dt,a˙t+Latψt=0,\mathcal W_K^2(a_0,a_1) \eqdef \inf_{a_t,\psi_t} \int_0^1\mathbb A_K(a_t,\psi_t)\,\d t, \qquad \dot a_t+\mathcal L_{a_t}\psi_t=0,WK2​(a0​,a1​):=at​,ψt​inf​∫01​AK​(at​,ψt​)dt,a˙t​+Lat​​ψt​=0,
(85)

with endpoint conditions at=0=a0a_{t=0}=a_0at=0​=a0​ and at=1=a1a_{t=1}=a_1at=1​=a1​. Equivalently, one can write the same formula in edge-flux variables: flux is only allowed along edges where Kij>0K_{ij}>0Kij​>0, and the denominator in the kinetic energy is the logarithmic mean of the two relative endpoint densities ρi(a)=ai/πi\rho_i(a)=a_i/\pi_iρi​(a)=ai​/πi​.

The first nontrivial finite Markov geometries already show how the logarithmic mean bends the simplex. In both examples below, take the uniform random walk on the complete neighbor graph, so πi=1/n\pi_i=1/nπi​=1/n and Kij=1/(n−1)K_{ij}=1/(n-1)Kij​=1/(n−1) for i≠ji\neq ji=j.

Example: Two-point complete graph

On Σ2\Sigma_2Σ2​, write a0=(r,1−r)a_0=(r,1-r)a0​=(r,1−r) and a1=(s,1−s)a_1=(s,1-s)a1​=(s,1−s). Since there is only one edge, the discrete dynamic problem reduces to the scalar Riemannian length

WK(a0,a1)=∣∫sr duθ(u,1−u)∣,0<r,s<1.\mathcal W_K(a_0,a_1) = \left|\int_s^r \frac{\d u}{\sqrt{\theta(u,1-u)}}\right|, \qquad 0<r,s<1.WK​(a0​,a1​)=∣∣​∫sr​θ(u,1−u)​du​∣∣​,0<r,s<1.
(86)

This formula is closed but not Euclidean: the logarithmic mean changes the cost of moving mass depending on the current split between the two points.

m12∗=h2/Θ23−h1/Θ13D,m13∗=−h1−m12∗,m23∗=m12∗−h2,m_{12}^*=\frac{h_2/\Theta_{23}-h_1/\Theta_{13}}{D}, \qquad m_{13}^*=-h_1-m_{12}^*, \qquad m_{23}^*=m_{12}^*-h_2,m12∗​=Dh2​/Θ23​−h1​/Θ13​​,m13∗​=−h1​−m12∗​,m23∗​=m12∗​−h2​,

and ∥h∥a2\|h\|_a^2∥h∥a2​ is obtained by inserting these values in (88). Therefore

WK2(a0,a1)=inf⁡at∈int⁡(Σ3)∫01∥a˙t∥at2  dt,at=0=a0,at=1=a1.\mathcal W_K^2(a_0,a_1) = \inf_{a_t\in\operatorname{int}(\Sigma_3)} \int_0^1\|\dot a_t\|_{a_t}^2\,\d t, \qquad a_{t=0}=a_0, \quad a_{t=1}=a_1.WK2​(a0​,a1​)=at​∈int(Σ3​)inf​∫01​∥a˙t​∥at​2​dt,at=0​=a0​,at=1​=a1​.

The formula is simple enough to compute directly, but it already shows the main difference with Euclidean geometry on the simplex: the local metric depends nonlinearly on the current density through logarithmic edge mobilities.

Dynamic Unbalanced OT¶

Balanced dynamic distances keep total mass fixed: their tangent variables are transport velocities or fluxes satisfying a continuity equation. Unbalanced distances use a different tangent model. A tangent variable now has both a spatial component and a reaction component, so mass can move, disappear and reappear. This reaction--transport geometry is introduced here before its use for gradient flows in Dynamic Unbalanced OT and WFR Flows.

Unbalanced dynamic transport is obtained by allowing mass to be created and destroyed along the path. The continuity equation is replaced by a balance equation, and the action penalizes both spatial motion and growth. This dynamic formulation underlies the Hellinger--Kantorovich and Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao metrics Liero et al., 2016Chizat et al., 2018; its equivalence with static entropy-transport and cone formulations is developed in Liero et al., 2018Chizat et al., 2018.

A representative quadratic action is

∂tρt+∇ ⁣⋅mt=st,∫01 ⁣∫(∣mt∣2ρt+κ2st2ρt) dx  dt,\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot m_t=s_t, \qquad \int_0^1\!\int \left(\frac{|m_t|^2}{\rho_t}+\kappa^2\frac{s_t^2}{\rho_t}\right)\d x\,\d t,∂t​ρt​+∇⋅mt​=st​,∫01​∫(ρt​∣mt​∣2​+κ2ρt​st2​​)dxdt,
(92)

with the usual perspective convention: zero flux and zero source through zero density cost nothing, whereas nonzero flux or source through zero density has infinite cost. Equivalently, writing mt=ρtvtm_t=\rho_t v_tmt​=ρt​vt​ and st=ρtgts_t=\rho_t g_tst​=ρt​gt​, one minimizes ∫01∫(∥vt∥2+κ2gt2)ρt  dx  dt\int_0^1\int(\norm{v_t}^2+\kappa^2 g_t^2)\rho_t\,\d x\,\d t∫01​∫(∥vt​∥2+κ2gt2​)ρt​dxdt under ∂tρt+∇ ⁣⋅(ρtvt)=gtρt\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\rho_t v_t)=g_t\rho_t∂t​ρt​+∇⋅(ρt​vt​)=gt​ρt​. The parameter κ\kappaκ fixes the relative cost of reaction and transport.

On the velocity side the pointwise action is

Aκ(a,w,g):=a(∥w∥2+κ2g2).A_\kappa(a,w,g) \eqdef a\bigl(\norm{w}^2+\kappa^2 g^2\bigr).Aκ​(a,w,g):=a(∥w∥2+κ2g2).
(93)

On the momentum side, with m=awm=awm=aw and r=agr=agr=ag, the three-variable perspective is

Jκ(a,m,r):={∥m∥2+κ2r2a,a>0,0,a=0, m=0, r=0,+∞,a=0, (m,r)≠(0,0).J_\kappa(a,m,r) \eqdef \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{\norm{m}^2+\kappa^2 r^2}{a}, & a>0,\\ 0, & a=0,\ m=0,\ r=0,\\ +\infty, & a=0,\ (m,r)\neq(0,0). \end{cases}Jκ​(a,m,r):=⎩⎨⎧​a∥m∥2+κ2r2​,0,+∞,​a>0,a=0, m=0, r=0,a=0, (m,r)=(0,0).​
(94)

For measure-valued triples, α\alphaα denotes the transported measure, μ\muμ the vector-valued flux measure, and σ\sigmaσ the signed source measure. If λ\lambdaλ dominates α\alphaα, ∣μ∣|\mu|∣μ∣ and ∣σ∣|\sigma|∣σ∣, define

Jκ(α,μ,σ):=∫Jκ ⁣( dα dλ, dμ dλ, dσ dλ) dλ.\mathbb J_\kappa(\alpha,\mu,\sigma) \eqdef \int J_\kappa\!\left( \frac{\d\alpha}{\d\lambda}, \frac{\d \mu}{\d\lambda}, \frac{\d \sigma}{\d\lambda} \right)\d\lambda .Jκ​(α,μ,σ):=∫Jκ​(dλdα​,dλdμ​,dλdσ​)dλ.
(95)

The one-homogeneity of JκJ_\kappaJκ​ makes this definition independent of the chosen dominating measure.

Proposition: Static/Dynamic Equivalence for Unbalanced OT

Fix the action above and let CWκ\mathcal C\mathcal W_\kappaCWκ​ be the cone value with the cone metric normalized to the same growth scale κ\kappaκ. For nonnegative finite measures α0,α1\alpha_0,\alpha_1α0​,α1​ on Rd\RR^dRd, the dynamic value

WFR⁡κ2(α0,α1):=inf⁡∂tαt+∇⋅μt=σtαt=0=α0, αt=1=α1∫01Jκ(αt,μt,σt)  dt\WFR_\kappa^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) \eqdef \inf_{\substack{\partial_t\alpha_t+\nabla\cdot \mu_t=\sigma_t\\ \alpha_{t=0}=\alpha_0,\ \alpha_{t=1}=\alpha_1}} \int_0^1 \mathbb J_\kappa(\alpha_t,\mu_t,\sigma_t)\,\d tWFRκ2​(α0​,α1​):=∂t​αt​+∇⋅μt​=σt​αt=0​=α0​, αt=1​=α1​​inf​∫01​Jκ​(αt​,μt​,σt​)dt
(96)

equals the static cone formulation CWκ(α0,α1)\mathcal C\mathcal W_\kappa(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)CWκ​(α0​,α1​). Hence the static unbalanced problem and the balance-equation least-action problem define the same geodesic distance.

Proof

The cone construction turns variation of mass into radial motion and spatial transport into angular motion on C[Rd]\mathfrak C[\RR^d]C[Rd]. Applying the Benamou--Brenier theorem on the cone to the lifted endpoint measures gives a dynamic least-action problem on C[Rd]\mathfrak C[\RR^d]C[Rd] whose static value is the cone value. Projecting a cone curve back to the base space with weight r2r^2r2 produces a measure curve, a spatial flux and a source term satisfying the balance equation. Conversely, any finite-action triple can be lifted to a cone curve with the same relaxed action. This gives the static/dynamic identity; see Liero et al., 2016Liero et al., 2018Chizat et al., 2018Chizat et al., 2018.

show_book_figure("dynamic-unbalanced-geodesic")

Balanced and unbalanced Sinkhorn-barycenter interpolations between two one-dimensional Gaussian mixtures with swapped modal masses. The balanced row conserves total mass, so excess mass from the dominant left mode must move along the line toward the dominant right target mode, producing transient mass in the middle. The unbalanced row uses KL-relaxed marginal constraints; mass can be attenuated near overrepresented modes and recreated near underrepresented modes, giving a reaction--transport interpolation closer to the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao intuition.
